details: Magnetic Materials: Substances strongly attracted by magnets (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt).
Non-magnetic Materials: Substances not attracted by magnets (wood, plastic, glass, rubber, copper, aluminum).
experiments_or_examples: Testing classroom objects (keys, pencils, erasers, clips) with a bar magnet

details: Magnetic attraction is concentrated at two ends called North Pole (N) and South Pole (S).
Magnetic force is weakest at the center of a bar magnet.
Magnetic poles always exist in inseparable pairs.
experiments_or_examples: Rolling a bar magnet in a heap of steel paperclips; maximum clips stick at the two ends

details: A freely suspended bar magnet always aligns itself along the geographic North-South direction.
Magnetic Compass: A pivoted magnetized needle inside a dial marked with cardinal directions (N, S, E, W).
Historical navigation: Early Indian sailors used the 'Matsya-yantra' (floating magnetic iron fish).
experiments_or_examples: Suspending a bar magnet using a thread and observing its resting direction

details: An unmagnetized iron piece (e.g., sewing needle) can be magnetized by stroking it repeatedly (30-40 times) in one direction using one fixed pole of a bar magnet.
experiments_or_examples: Stroking an iron needle with a bar magnet and floating it on a cork in water to act as a compass

branches.theme: 4.5 Laws of Magnetism and Care of Magnets

details: Like poles repel each other (N-N repels, S-S repels).
Opposite poles attract each other (N-S attracts).
Repulsion is the only conclusive test for magnetism.
Demagnetization occurs due to heating, hammering, dropping, or improper storage.
experiments_or_examples: Bringing two bar magnets close on toy cars; observing attraction vs push-back repulsion
Storing magnets in pairs with opposite poles separated by wood and soft iron keepers
